nameStory: The name 'thimbleweed' comes from the plant's distinctive cylindrical seed head that looks remarkably like an old-fashioned sewing thimble. After the small greenish-white flowers fade away, this fuzzy, elongated cluster of seeds becomes the plant's most recognizable feature. The word 'cylindrical' in its scientific name refers to this same thimble-like shape that makes it stand out among other wildflowers.
description: Cylindrical thimbleweed is a prairie wildflower that forms small clumps and grows 1-3 feet tall on sturdy, upright stems. Its small greenish-white flowers bloom in early summer but aren't particularly showy. What makes this plant memorable is what happens after flowering - it develops a distinctive fuzzy, gray-white seed head that looks exactly like a sewing thimble perched on top of the stem. This hardy member of the buttercup family is quite rare in New England, with only a handful of known locations.

idTips.label: Seed Head
idTips.description: The cylindrical, thimble-shaped seed head is covered in dense, woolly gray-white fluff that feels soft to the touch - this is the plant's signature feature that persists long after flowers fade

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish-white flowers with 5-8 petal-like sepals that feel papery and lack the bright colors typical of buttercup family members

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small clumps with multiple upright stems reaching 1-3 feet tall, often growing in colonies connected by underground roots

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided leaves that feel slightly rough and are arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem, typically with 3 main leaflets that are further subdivided

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Individual seeds have long, silky white hairs that catch the wind and feel cottony when rubbed between fingers - they blow away like dandelion seeds

habitat: This prairie species prefers dry, open areas with well-drained soils, including old fields, meadows, and disturbed sites along roadsides. In New England, it's extremely rare and typically found in areas that mimic its native prairie habitat, such as sunny grasslands or openings in dry woodlands. It thrives in full sun and can tolerate poor, sandy soils where many other wildflowers struggle.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as distinctive whorled leaves appear on upright stems, making the plant identifiable even before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: Small greenish-white flowers bloom from early to late summer, followed by the development of the characteristic cylindrical seed heads that become increasingly prominent.
seasonality.fall: The fuzzy gray-white thimble-shaped seed heads are at their most conspicuous, releasing their cottony seeds on windy days while the foliage begins to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried seed heads still visible, though the distinctive thimble shape becomes less obvious as seeds disperse.

funFact: Each of those fluffy seed heads contains dozens of individual seeds, and every single fluffy strand is actually a modified style - the female part of the flower that's grown into a personal parachute to carry the seed away on the wind, sometimes for miles across the landscape.
confusionNotes: The cylindrical seed head distinguishes it from tall thimbleweed, which has a more rounded, globe-shaped seed head that looks less like an actual thimble. Remember: cylindrical thimbleweed has a seed head shaped like a narrow thimble, while tall thimbleweed's seed head is more like a fuzzy ball.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'thimbleweed,' this plant is actually in the buttercup family and is more closely related to pasque flowers and windflowers than to true weeds. Several different species share the common name 'thimbleweed,' which can cause confusion when trying to identify them without using scientific names.
compareHints: Cylindrical thimbleweed differs from its relative tall thimbleweed by its distinctly elongated, narrow seed head versus the latter's more rounded, globe-shaped one. While both have similar small greenish-white flowers and whorled leaves, the cylindrical species is much rarer in New England. Cutleaf anemone is typically smaller overall and has more finely divided, ferny-looking leaves compared to the broader leaflets of cylindrical thimbleweed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tall thimbleweed stands out from its relatives by its height and that distinctive whorl of three deeply cut leaves halfway up the stem.
Unlike its New England relatives tall thimbleweed and cylindrical thimbleweed, cutleaf anemone has much more finely divided, lacy leaves rather than broader, coarsely toothed ones.
